Crew from NASA's simulated Mars mission emerges after 378 days in isolation

Nov 1 : The four members of a crew who took part in a simulated mission to Mars have emerged after 378 days in isolation at the US space agency's Johnson Space Center in Houston, an endeavor designed to help prepare for a possible future excursion by NASA astronauts to Earth's planetary neighbor. "It's been a hell of a year — analog astronauts living in captivity of our own free will," Ellen Ellis, the medical officer on the Crew Health and Performance Exploration Analog, or CHAPEA, mission, said in remarks at Johnson Space Center after emerging with her three crewmates on Saturday. The four entered the 1,700-square-foot (158-square-meter) 3D-printed habitat on October 19, 2025, and performed tasks such as growing crops in simulated Martian soil and interfacing with NASA officials with delays recreating those inherent in interplanetary communications. NASA, which has explored Mars with robotic rovers and orbiting spacecraft, has ambitions for a human mission to Mars as early as the 2030s, with plans before that to return astronauts to the moon for the first time since 1972.

"We have a narrowing window of opportunity to maintain US preeminence in space," Ellis said. Ellis mentioned the service academy for space-related operations pursued by President Donald Trump's administration and plans for a lunar base. "Let's seize the initiative, lead with science that will benefit our economy and ensure our legacy in space for our children's children," Ellis said. The other crew members were mission commander Ross Elder, science officer Matthew Montgomery and flight engineer James Spicer. "For Mars, the risks are great," Elder said in remarks after emerging from isolation. "But through seeking understanding, strong vision and leadership, creativity, fortitude, hard work and incredible foundation, the goal of putting humans on Mars is not only achievable, but rather inevitable." The crew is set to participate in two weeks of post-mission evaluations and debriefing with NASA scientists. NASA has said it is looking for insight into what it takes for astronauts to adapt to the routines and demands of daily life on long-duration missions beyond Earth to keep them healthy, productive, and connected. This was NASA's second CHAPEA mission, with another four-person crew in isolation at Johnson Space Center for 378 days spanning 2023 and 2024. Vanessa Wyche, director of the Johnson Space Center, greeted the crew members when they exited isolation. Wyche said they managed to live with limited resources, maintain their habitat, and carry out simulated Mars operations.  Wyche also noted how the crew dealt with the simulated interplanetary communications, with lag times between sending messages and receiving responses. "These delays require patience, careful planning and greater independence — qualities that will be essential for future astronauts traveling millions of miles from home," Wyche said. Wyche said the lessons learned from the CHAPEA crew and their experiences will help pave the way for the missions first to the moon and "one day, Mars."

Source: Reuters

LONDON/MOSCOW, Nov 1 : OPEC+ oil-producing countries kept December production targets steady on Sunday, confirming expectations that more policy adjustments will not occur until next year, as the group continues to struggle with export disruptions from the Iran war. Seven core OPEC+ members — Saudi Arabia, Russia, Iraq, Kuwait, Algeria, Kazakhstan and Oman — made the decision in an online meeting on Sunday, OPEC said in a statement. While Gulf members have been boosting exports that have been disrupted for months by the conflict, most are still pumping well below their targets. OPEC+ comprises the Organization of the Petroleum Exporting Countries and allies including Russia. Only the seven members — plus the United Arab Emirates until it quit OPEC in May — have been involved in monthly output decisions in recent years. All members of the 21-country group are due to meet on November 29, when analysts expect it will decide 2027 quotas. "Today's decision was the easy one," said Jorge Leon, an analyst at Rystad. "The much more important test comes at the November 29 ministerial meeting, when OPEC+ will decide its 2027 production framework."

Oil prices jumped more than 2 per cent on Friday, with Brent crude settling at almost $118 a barrel, the highest since April, as traders braced for a potential escalation in the Iran war after the US midterm elections. The International Energy Agency and other forecasters have warned of excess supply in 2027 should Gulf flows return to normal. "OPEC+ faces an extremely difficult call for 2027," Leon added. "The group has to plan around huge uncertainty over the US-Iran war, the pace of recovery through the Strait of Hormuz, and the size of the surplus that could emerge once disrupted barrels return." OIL CAPACITY REVIEW IN FOCUS The seven members have been boosting output targets for much of 2026 and in September completed the phased rollback of a 1.65 million-barrel-per-day supply cut first agreed in 2023. At earlier meetings, they kept the targets steady for October and November. OPEC+ still has one more layer of production cuts of about 2 million bpd covering most members through the end of 2026. The group needs to complete a review of members' production capacity during the fourth quarter before setting the 2027 baselines that will determine future quotas and shape plans to unwind those cuts, sources have said. The Iran war has disrupted projects to expand capacity across the Middle East, throwing estimates of future production potential into uncertainty, Reuters reported in October. As a result, the review is now expected to be completed by mid-November. (Writing by Alex Lawler; Editing by Joe Bavier and Alex Richardson)

Source: Reuters

SEOUL, Nov 1 : South Korea's exports nearly doubled in October from a year earlier, beating market expectations and marking the sharpest jump in more than 50 years, trade data showed on Sunday. Exports from Asia's fourth-largest economy, a bellwether for global trade, rose 93.7 per cent last month to $115.28 billion, slightly higher than a median 93.2 per cent rise forecast in a Reuters poll of economists. The increase, boosted by favourable calendar effects of more working days due to the timing difference in local Chuseok holidays, beat September's 83.7 per cent gain and was the strongest since January 1974. Overseas sales of semiconductors jumped 259.4 per cent as prices and volume remained high on continued facility investment by global big tech firms in the competition for artificial intelligence industry leadership, the trade ministry said.

Binance, the world's biggest cryptocurrency exchange, resumed bitcoin, ether and some stablecoin withdrawals on Sunday (Nov 1) and said others would follow in phases, after it covered 95 per cent of the US$6.3 billion in tokens stolen from its platform. The heist, which the FBI has tied to North Korea and analysts believe may be the biggest financial robbery ever, adds to a string of recent crypto thefts. Last year, attackers stole US$2.9 billion worth of cryptocurrency across nearly 150 attacks, according to researchers at TRM Labs. Binance, which was founded in China, said the first phase of withdrawals would cover 15 crypto assets including bitcoin, ether, XRP and dogecoin. Bitcoin withdrawals resumed shortly after 0600 GMT, while ether, BNB and some USDT and USDC stablecoin withdrawals were also restored. Binance said it had covered US$6 billion of stolen cryptocurrencies by using company money to buy replacement tokens. The remaining 5 per cent of stolen tokens consist of assets that are less liquid and may take longer to source in the required amounts, according to the exchange. FBI TIES ATTACK TO NORTH KOREAN UNIT

The FBI said on Saturday that the North Korean state-sponsored unit known as TraderTraitor was responsible for the attack. Pyongyang has for years denied using state-linked cyber units for espionage, financial theft and revenue. Its mission in Geneva and embassy in China did not respond to requests for comment. Law enforcement observed members of the unit converting stolen assets into the cryptocurrency ether, the FBI said in a statement, adding that it expected "further laundering" of the assets through the use of related technology. Analysts had also blamed North Korea for the heist. The bulk of the theft unfolded in around 20 minutes beginning late on Thursday and bore similarities to previous large attacks blamed on North Korea, according to US blockchain analysis firms TRM Labs and Chainalysis. US President Donald Trump, however, said on Saturday that the United States was still not certain if North Korea was involved. "We don't know if it's North Korea - but if it is, we'll talk to North Korea about it," Trump told reporters on Saturday in comments posted by a White House account on X.

Related:

Gone in 20 minutes: How the biggest heist in crypto history unfolded

BINANCE VOWS TO BEAR FINANCIAL COSTS Binance has been working with industry partners to freeze some of the affected assets, with about US$3 billion located as of Friday, it said. The exchange has repeatedly said it would bear the financial impact of the funds stolen in the hack. It has set aside around US$6.34 billion of company funds internally to cover the losses. The money spent buying replacement tokens came from Binance's US$1 billion Secure Asset Fund for Users (SAFU), a bitcoin reserve it holds to protect customers in the event of security breaches, as well as some of its Futures Insurance Fund and its corporate treasury, it said on X. Co-CEO Yi He said on Saturday that 50 per cent of its SAFU funds would be used, while the company committed to replenishing the fund to about US$1 billion. Richard Teng, the other co-CEO, has said that the breach was a "complex attack" involving a compromised laptop and malicious software designed to delete evidence of its activity, making it harder to trace and investigate. Crypto prices fell on Friday, while Binance sought to reassure customers that their funds were safe after the hack. Binance, which allows users to buy, sell and trade digital assets, has 335 million registered users globally and had about US$162.8 billion in assets under custody as of its 2025 annual report. BINANCE FOUNDER CZ THANKS US LAW ENFORCEMENT In a post on X that quoted the FBI statement on North Korea’s involvement, Binance thanked the agency for its support. It did not respond to a request for comment on North Korea's involvement. Binance founder Changpeng Zhao, who was convicted in the US of failing to maintain an effective anti-money laundering program before being pardoned by Trump last year, said US law enforcement agencies provided vital help, including by tracking and freezing the stolen assets. "A tweet can't fully express our gratitude. Many crypto bros may not realize, a lot of the 'why bitcoin didn't drop more?' credit goes to them," Zhao wrote, referring to the US law enforcement agencies.

Related:

Hackers allegedly from North Korea steal US$6.3 billion from Binance in world's biggest crypto heist

Source: Reuters/fs/ht

The remaining 10 per cent consists of tokens that are less liquid, meaning they may take longer to buy, it said in a statement posted on X. "We've now replenished 90 per cent of the stolen assets, and we're committed to covering the remaining 10 per cent. Our users will not bear the financial impact of this incident," co-CEO Richard Teng said on X on Saturday.  Crypto prices fell on Friday, while Binance — the world's biggest crypto exchange — sought to reassure customers that their funds were safe after losing more than $6 billion worth of crypto in a hack that analysts and the FBI blamed on North Korea.

NEW YORK, Oct 31 : US electricity prices had flown under the radar in past national elections, but they have become a major political issue in this year's midterms as Americans grow angry over rising utility bills and deals for power-hungry data centers. Nationwide, according to Energy Information Administration data, electricity prices for homes have risen more than 10 per cent since 2024 when President Donald Trump was elected along with Republican majorities in both houses of the US Congress. Higher electricity prices have outpaced the rise in costs for other goods and services. Power bills have grown even faster in political battleground states of Ohio, Michigan and Pennsylvania, which are also hot spots for new data centers. In some cases, electricity bills have soared by triple the inflation rate.  Many politicians vying for top statehouse seats across the country this year have backed cracking down on utilities. Some have proposed freezing utility rate increases and slashing guaranteed returns, steps that could have sweeping consequences for the country's utility industry.

"It could be the first election to feature utilities and electricity, specifically, as a prominent issue in the midterms," said Charles Hua, executive director of PowerLines, a nonprofit that advocates reforming utility policy to favor consumers. "Part of that is because people's utility bills have gone up and up, and they don't see any end in sight."  Utilities are heavily regulated. State regulators generally must approve utilities’ requests to spend on the grid and to recover those costs through rate increases. Regulators also set the return on equity utilities can earn on their grid investments.  This year, utilities are on track to match last year's record high $31 billion in rate increase requests to regulators, a PowerLines survey showed.  Last year's spending was double the previous record. The investor-owned companies are also expected to carry out a record of nearly $1.3 trillion in capital spending over the next five years, according to an analysis by S&P Global’s Regulatory Research Associates. UTILITIES SPOTLIGHTED Seats on nine state public utility commissions are up for election this year, nearly all the US states where voters elect their utility regulators. These include burgeoning data center hubs Arizona and Georgia. Governors will be chosen in 36 US states this year, and governors appoint utility regulators in states where commissioners are not directly elected.  In Ohio, Democrat Amy Acton has promised to lower energy bills if she is elected governor. Her campaign said she will also appoint a public utilities commission that was "not beholden to utility companies" and work with the state attorney general to crack down on "excessive rate hikes and predatory practices." Ohio's residential electricity bills have grown by more than 20 per cent over the last two years, according to EIA data. Acton has also said she supports a data center moratorium. Her Republican opponent Vivek Ramaswamy said he would assure Ohioans living near data centers would not pay electricity bills at all. BULLY PULPIT Some governors who are up for reelection have used their political weight to pressure the power industry to keep prices down. In April, Pennsylvania Governor Josh Shapiro announced that prominent utility, PECO Energy Company, had acceded to his demand that it withdraw its proposal with state regulators to increase rates. Shapiro, a Democrat running for reelection, said the move would reduce future utility bills by as much as $34 a month. He followed up with a letter to more utility CEOs seeking changes in how utilities justify spending and returns on equity. "The governors are using this crisis on energy affordability as an opportunity to take a deeper dive into the utility regulatory model and see if it makes any sense," said Jamie Van Nostrand, senior fellow at the Kleinman Center for Energy Policy at the University of Pennsylvania and former chair of the Massachusetts Department of Public Utilities.  Power bills tracked low inflation for roughly a decade, and were not an issue in most mainstream elections until last year, when Mikie Sherrill successfully ran for New Jersey governor on the promise of freezing utility bills. She did so the same day she took office. In Virginia, home to the largest concentration of data centers in the world, Governor Abigail Spanberger took a similar approach, which industry analysts said could offer a playbook for those who win this year’s elections.  Utility advocates say reducing guaranteed returns and freezing rates will not make a meaningful difference in household bills but could lead to a long-term reduction of investments in the grid. "The grid is America's greatest machine, and it doesn't operate on the political calendar,” said Drew Maloney, president of Edison Electric Institute, a trade organization for investor-owned electric utilities. “It requires consistent investment every year to deliver reliable energy to our customers." Credit rating agency Fitch downgraded the North American utility sector to "deteriorating" from "neutral" in June, citing political pressure in the midterms to limit electricity bills and utility profits. For an industry that plans in decades, it is hard to predict the result of short-term political moves aimed at saving money for households. "I do think the real meat will come after the election," Hua said.

Source: Reuters

WASHINGTON: HKT, a leading Hong Kong telecom carrier and subsidiary of PCCW Ltd, on Friday (Oct 30) agreed to halt its operations in the United States under pressure from the Federal Communications Commission. The FCC in October 2025 said it was moving to revoke the authority of HKT to operate in the United States, citing national security concerns and its affiliation with China Unicom, which is a shareholder in PCCW. Under a consent decree reviewed by Reuters, HKT has agreed to stop international and domestic telecom services to and within the United States. HKT must file an application with the FCC within 30 days to discontinue services and must discontinue US services by September 1, 2027. PCCW declined immediate comment. The agreement means the FCC will not move forward with the revocation proceeding that could have offered more details on Washington's national security concerns.

The FCC has previously barred China Mobile, China Telecom and China Unicom from providing international telecommunications services to the United States, citing broad national security concerns. The Trump administration has continued an extensive crackdown on Chinese telecoms over the past year. The FCC on Thursday voted to ban all Chinese labs from testing US electronics starting from December 2028. The telecom crackdown has sparked a strong reaction from Beijing. China said Friday it firmly opposes the FCC action on labs, warning it would take necessary countermeasures "if the US side persists in acting unilaterally". The FCC also announced on Thursday it plans to soon ban Chinese telecom firms from direct access to US phone numbers on national security grounds. The plan would bar Chinese IP network service providers from direct access and those that use equipment from companies on the FCC's list that pose national security risks, including Huawei and ZTE. Other measures under consideration by the FCC include barring Chinese telecom firms from connecting to US networks and from operating their data centers in the US.  Concerns about the potential for spying and other harms to arise from Chinese access to US telecom data and infrastructure have grown in recent years. In late 2024, Washington said a Chinese state-sponsored cyber espionage group known as Salt Typhoon stole consumers' call records and US call data and infiltrated US telecommunications and telecom infrastructure firms. China has consistently denied any wrongdoing.

BEIJING: China's factory activity unexpectedly dropped in October, its third contraction in four months, a government survey showed on Saturday (Oct 31), hurt by soft demand for exports as well as goods at home. The official manufacturing purchasing managers' index (PMI) fell to 49.3 from 50.1 in September, according to data from the National Bureau of Statistics. That missed a forecast for 50.0 from a Reuters poll. Factory activity weakened as overseas Christmas-related orders, which were front-loaded in September, cooled in October. It was also hurt when consumer spending, which climbed during China's long National Day holiday in the first week of October, fizzled out after, in a return to its long-stagnant state. "Insufficient demand is increasing downward pressure on the economy," said Zhang Liqun, an analyst with the China Federation of Logistics & Purchasing, adding that policymakers should take the problem seriously and step up measures as soon as possible.

Sub-indexes for new orders overall and for new export orders both stayed in contraction territory in October. Production and purchasing activity also slipped into contraction from expansion. The non-manufacturing PMI, which covers services and construction, also dropped to 49.7 from 50.2 in September. The readings are compiled based on purchasing managers' reports about whether conditions improved, worsened or were unchanged in areas such as new orders, output and employment compared with the previous month. A reading above 50 signals expansion, while one below 50 indicates contraction. Some sectors within manufacturing were doing well. Production and new orders sub-indexes for railway, shipbuilding, aerospace equipment, and computer, communications and electronics manufacturing were all at or above 53.0, the survey showed. AI-related firms in particular have reported strong earnings growth. Zhongji Innolight, a maker of high-speed optical modules that connect servers and switches in AI data centres, posted a near tripling in third-quarter net profit. But the lacklustre domestic market and rising costs have weighed on many old-school manufacturers and property-linked firms. Custom furniture maker Oppein Home, for example, saw net profit plunge 80 per cent during the quarter. China's economy is, however, expected to meet the country's 4.5-5.0 per cent annual growth target without additional stimulus measures after third-quarter growth rebounded to 4.5 per cent from 4.3 per cent in April-June.

Oct 30 : Crypto exchanges are taking quick action to bolster their defenses and urging greater industry-wide information-sharing after a record $6.3 billion hack of Binance exposed their vulnerability just as they become more embedded in mainstream finance. Coinbase said it made adjustments to its systems that store cryptocurrency keys offline "solely out of an abundance of caution," while Kraken said it was monitoring industry incidents for lessons it could apply to its defenses. But the industry will need to move urgently, analysts and industry executives said, as President Donald Trump's regulators promote deeper integration of digital assets into the financial system, raising the stakes for an industry with a history of big hacks. "For crypto to reach its full potential, the security situation must be addressed immediately," said Chris Perkins, Franklin Templeton's head of crypto.

Binance, the world's largest crypto exchange, halted withdrawals after Thursday's attack — which analysts blamed on North Korea — and said it would use company funds to cover the losses. Binance co-CEO Richard Teng said on X that the “complex attack” may have begun with a compromised software engineer’s laptop, giving hackers access to systems used to process withdrawals. The company later found additional breaches, while software designed to erase traces of the attack hampered the investigation. Rival crypto exchanges moved quickly on Friday to shore up their own systems and to reassure customers that their tokens were safe “Full-time teams at Kraken look for potential vulnerabilities every day,” a Kraken spokesperson said. Still, even as the industry reeled from the biggest cryptocurrency heist of all time, executives expressed confidence that Binance had sufficient resources to cover the losses and that the hack would not have broader financial repercussions. Bitcoin fell more than 4 per cent on Thursday while ether, the second-largest cryptocurrency, fell more than 5 per cent, although both tokens recovered some of that ground on Friday. "Our expectation is the industry writ large will actually not suffer material losses, even though Binance is obviously going to have to deal with the exploit directly," said Josh Riezman, chief legal and strategy officer at crypto firm GSR. The bulk of the heist unfolded in around 20 minutes late on Thursday and bore similarities to previous attacks blamed on North Korea, according to US blockchain analysis firms TRM Labs and Chainalysis. North Korea routinely denies involvement in cryptocurrency thefts, and its mission in Geneva did not respond to requests for comment. HACK INVOLVES SOCIAL ENGINEERING, MONEY LAUNDERING While much remains unclear, social engineering, a common tactic in which hackers trick victims into revealing sensitive information or granting access to systems, may have been involved in compromising the laptop, security experts said. Harry Donnelly, CEO of Circuit, a crypto risk infrastructure company, said companies are planning more employee training to guard against social engineering attacks. In such attacks, hackers race to launder the funds before the exchange detects the breach and token issuers freeze assets. Stablecoin issuer Tether said it had frozen nearly $1.57 billion linked to Binance, while Circle said it froze $800 million. Bitcoin and ether cannot be frozen because no single entity controls the coins. Chainalysis said the hackers appeared to be using sophisticated laundering patterns it had not seen before. On Friday, some crypto exchange executives called for the industry to develop a coordinated hack detection system. "We need a real-time alert system that allows participants to share information immediately when a hack occurs, coordinate a rapid response, and temporarily freeze suspected stolen funds," said Star Xu, CEO of crypto exchange OKX, in a post on X. GSR's Riezman added that the Binance hack could spur the industry to act: "As we're at this kind of confluence moment for traditional finance and digital assets, I think it's obviously important that we continue to improve, and I think this, if anything, will be a catalyst for that."

Source: Reuters

Oct 30 : OpenAI has slashed the target for its latest funding round by $10 billion amid a selloff in tech stocks driven by AI worries, the Financial Times reported on Friday, citing people with knowledge of the matter. The ChatGPT maker is now seeking about $20 billion and its desired valuation has dropped to $1.25 trillion from $1.4 billion, the report said. OpenAI set a Friday deadline for investors to commit to the funding round, but the "first close" is expected to raise less than $20 billion after some investors reduced their allocations, it added. A consortium of UAE investors that includes state-backed technology fund MGX is expected to be the largest participant in the round, and as part of the deal, OpenAI would gain the option to lease newly developed computing capacity in the region, the newspaper added.

Oct 30 : S&P Global Ratings on Friday revised its outlook on Meta Platforms to "negative" from "stable", citing significant uncertainty around the social media giant's capital spending and free operating cash flow. Big Tech has historically spent heavily on cloud computing, online advertising and e-commerce, but the AI boom has pushed capital expenditure to dizzying levels, stoking investor concerns about whether the sector can generate returns quickly enough. Last week, Meta forecast annual capital expenditure between $135 billion-$145 billion after reporting a free cash flow deficit of $2.12 billion in the third quarter. Meta is also planning to tap public markets and sell $97.5 billion in stock to fund the AI buildout. Meta's ability to monetize its AI investments is more limited than that of its peers, S&P said, adding it was unclear when its revenue streams would generate material contributions exceeding their rising costs over the next few years.

S&P now forecasts Meta will generate FOCF deficits of $39 billion in 2026 and $71 billion in 2027. The agency said elevated spending could keep FOCF negative beyond 2028 and expects Meta to fund its 2028 cash shortfall entirely with debt. "Given the lack of clarity around the company's future capex and its very ambitious multi-year AI investment plans, we are less certain that it will curtail its spending as previously anticipated," S&P said. The ratings agency said it believes Meta's leverage could rise to above 1.0x as early as 2027, which is S&P Global's threshold for the "AA-" issuer credit rating. "We respectfully disagree with S&P's assertion about Meta's AI monetization capabilities," a Meta spokesperson told Reuters, adding that the company sees "significant product and business opportunities ahead of us, supporting our very strong credit profile." Meta's leverage increased from 0.1x in 2025, primarily due to its strategy of leasing data-center capacity rather than issuing debt, S&P said. "If capex remains elevated and continues to grow at a faster pace than we expect, credit profiles will continue to weaken and cash flows will be negative," Naveen Sarma, US media and telecom sector lead at S&P Global Ratings, said. The company reported long-term debt of $80.92 billion as of September 30. S&P on Thursday also lowered its outlook on Broadcom to stable from positive, saying the chipmaker's rapid AI growth was increasing its exposure to a few big customers. Earlier this year, S&P lowered cloud computing giant Oracle's credit rating to "BBB-", one notch above "junk", due to its heavily leveraged balance sheet.

Source: Reuters
